pairs.source_text: initium et causa penes Aelium Seianum cohortibus praetoriis praefectum cuius de potentia supra memoravi.
pairs.question: Quod munus apud Tiberium gerebat L. Aelius Seianus, ut initio libri quarti Annalium Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: What office did Lucius Aelius Sejanus hold under Tiberius, as Tacitus reports at the start of book 4 of the Annals?
pairs.answer_en: Prefect of the praetorian cohorts (the praetorian prefect).
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Sejanus + Tiberius; single office, supported verbatim by 'penes Aelium Seianum cohortibus praetoriis praefectum'. Closed-book: Sejanus as Tiberius's praetorian prefect is among the best-known facts of the reign. Answer rendered in the nominative as a title.

pairs.source_text: genitus Vulsiniis patre Seio Strabone equite Romano, et prima iuventa Gaium Caesarem divi Augusti nepotem sectatus
pairs.question: Quo in oppido Aelium Seianum natum esse Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: In what town does Tacitus report that Aelius Sejanus was born?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Sejanus; single place, supported verbatim by 'genitus Vulsiniis'. Locative. Closed-book: Sejanus's Etruscan origin at Volsinii is a stock biographical fact.

pairs.source_text: genitus Vulsiniis patre Seio Strabone equite Romano, et prima iuventa Gaium Caesarem divi Augusti nepotem sectatus
pairs.question: Quis fuit pater Aelii Seiani, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: Who was the father of Aelius Sejanus, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Sejanus; single named person, supported verbatim by 'patre Seio Strabone equite Romano'. Closed-book: Seius Strabo (himself a praetorian prefect) as Sejanus's father is a stock fact.

pairs.source_text: Vim praefecturae modicam antea intendit, dispersas per urbem cohortis una in castra conducendo, ut simul imperia acciperent numeroque et robore et visu inter se fiducia ipsis, in ceteros metus oreretur.
pairs.question: In quot castra Seianus cohortes praetorias antea per urbem dispersas conduxit, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: Into how many camps did Sejanus gather the praetorian cohorts that had previously been scattered through the city, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: The famous institutional fact: Sejanus concentrated the scattered praetorian cohorts into a single camp at Rome (the Castra Praetoria). Anchored to Sejanus + the praetorian cohorts; supported verbatim by 'dispersas per urbem cohortis una in castra conducendo'. 'castra' is plural in form but denotes one camp; the answer mirrors the text's 'una in castra'.

pairs.source_text: Igitur Seianus maturandum ratus deligit venenum quo paulatim inrepente fortuitus morbus adsimularetur. id Druso datum per Lygdum spadonem, ut octo post annos cognitum est.
pairs.question: Per quem ministrum venenum Druso, Tiberii filio, datum esse Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: Through what servant does Tacitus report that the poison was given to Drusus, Tiberius's son?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Drusus (Tiberius's son) + the poisoning; single named agent, supported verbatim by 'id Druso datum per Lygdum spadonem'. Closed-book: the poisoning of Drusus through Sejanus's agency, discovered eight years later, is a stock fact of the reign.

pairs.source_text: igitur cuncta temptanti promptissimum visum ad uxorem eius Liviam convertere, quae soror Germanici, formae initio aetatis indecorae, mox pulchritudine praecellebat.
pairs.question: Cuius soror erat Livia, uxor Drusi, quam Seianus in adulterium pellexit, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: Whose sister was Livia, the wife of Drusus, whom Sejanus enticed into adultery, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Livia (Livilla), wife of Drusus + Sejanus; single named relation, supported verbatim by 'uxorem eius Liviam ... quae soror Germanici' ('eius' = Drusus). Closed-book: Livilla, sister of Germanicus and wife of Drusus, seduced by Sejanus as his accomplice in the poisoning, is a stock fact.

pairs.source_text: Cornelio Cosso Asinio Agrippa consulibus Cremutius Cordus postulatur novo ac tunc primum audito crimine, quod editis annalibus laudatoque M. Bruto C. Cassium Romanorum ultimum dixisset.
pairs.question: Quem Cremutius Cordus, editis annalibus, Romanorum ultimum dixisse accusatus est, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: Whom was Cremutius Cordus accused of having called 'the last of the Romans' in his published annals, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Cremutius Cordus + his annals; single named person, supported verbatim by 'C. Cassium Romanorum ultimum dixisset'. Closed-book: Cremutius Cordus's prosecution for praising Brutus and calling Cassius the last of the Romans is among the most famous episodes of literary repression under Tiberius.

pairs.source_text: egressus dein senatu vitam abstinentia finivit. libros per aedilis cremandos censuere patres: set manserunt, occultati et editi.
pairs.question: Quid de libris Cremutii Cordi senatus censuit, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: What did the senate decree concerning the books of Cremutius Cordus, per Tacitus?
pairs.answer_en: That they be burned by the aediles.
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Cremutius Cordus's books + the senate; supported verbatim by 'libros per aedilis cremandos censuere patres'. Closed-book: the burning of Cremutius Cordus's books (which Tacitus notes survived in hiding) is a stock fact. Answer rendered as an indirect-command clause.

pairs.source_text: nam coepto apud Fidenam amphitheatro Atilius quidam libertini generis, quo spectaculum gladiatorum celebraret, neque fundamenta per solidum subdidit neque firmis nexibus ligneam compagem superstruxit
pairs.question: In quo oppido fuit amphitheatrum, a libertino Atilio exstructum, quod ruina ingentem stragem dedit, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: In what town was the amphitheatre, built by the freedman Atilius, whose collapse caused a huge disaster, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to the freedman Atilius + the amphitheatre disaster; single place, supported verbatim by 'coepto apud Fidenam amphitheatro Atilius quidam libertini generis'. Closed-book: the collapse of the amphitheatre at Fidenae is a famous disaster of Tiberius's reign.

pairs.source_text: quinquaginta hominum milia eo casu debilitata vel obtrita sunt; cautumque in posterum senatus consulto ne quis gladiatorium munus ederet cui minor quadringentorum milium res neve amphitheatrum imponeretur nisi solo firmitatis spectatae.
pairs.question: Quot hominum milia ruina amphitheatri Fidenatis debilitata vel obtrita esse Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: How many thousands of people does Tacitus say were maimed or crushed by the collapse of the amphitheatre at Fidenae?
pairs.derivation: The famous toll of the Fidenae amphitheatre disaster. Anchored to the Fidenae collapse; single number, supported verbatim by 'quinquaginta hominum milia eo casu debilitata vel obtrita sunt'. Closed-book number fact.

pairs.source_text: perosus tamen municipia et colonias omniaque in continenti sita Capreas se in insulam abdidit trium milium freto ab extremis Surrentini promunturii diiunctam.
pairs.question: In quam insulam Tiberius, relictis municipiis et continenti, se abdidit, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: To what island did Tiberius withdraw, leaving the towns and the mainland, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Tiberius; single named place, supported verbatim by 'Capreas se in insulam abdidit'. Closed-book: Tiberius's retirement to Capri is among the best-known facts of his reign.

pairs.source_text: Ceterum Tiberius neptem Agrippinam Germanico ortam cum coram Cn. Domitio tradidisset, in urbe celebrari nuptias iussit.
pairs.question: Cui Tiberius Agrippinam, Germanico ortam, in matrimonium tradidit, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: To whom did Tiberius give Agrippina, daughter of Germanicus, in marriage, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Tiberius + Agrippina the Younger, daughter of Germanicus; single named person, supported verbatim by 'neptem Agrippinam Germanico ortam cum coram Cn. Domitio tradidisset'. Closed-book: the marriage of Agrippina the Younger to Cn. Domitius Ahenobarbus, the future parents of the emperor Nero, is a stock genealogical fact; this is the closing sentence of book 4.

pairs.source_text: differtur per manipulos, Tacfarinatem omnes notum tot proeliis consectentur: non nisi duce interfecto requiem belli fore. at ille deiectis circum stipatoribus vinctoque iam filio et effusis undique Romanis ruendo in tela captivitatem haud inulta morte effugit; isque finis armis impositus.
pairs.question: Cuius ducis interitu diuturnum bellum Africanum sub Tiberio confectum esse Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: By the death of what leader does Tacitus say the long African war under Tiberius was brought to an end?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Tacfarinas + the African war; single named person, supported by 'non nisi duce interfecto requiem belli fore' and 'isque finis armis impositus' (Tacfarinas fell rushing into the Roman weapons rather than be captured). Closed-book: Tacfarinas, the Numidian leader of the long revolt in Africa, is a recurring figure whose death ended the war in this year.
